chapter_theme: The Vidyadhara host comes down from the sky to meet the Podanam king's host, and the two armies mingle like rivers and seas; the kings embrace and bow, Arkakirti is raised onto the king's elephant, and the party enters the city to the Chitrakuta hall, where the king begins to speak.

cast.role: the Vidyadhara king, lord of the hill, bride's father
the king of Podanam, named only by epithets, read as Tivittan's father
Arkakirti, son of the Vidyadhara king
the conch-coloured youth, read as Vijayan
the sea-dark youth, read as Tivittan
the host of the Podanam king
the women of the hill-clans who travel with the host
the Vidyadhara king's nephew or son-in-law
a hero named Sripalan, whose relation is unclear
the two kings and the princes together
the women who bless and fan the kings in the palace

947.reading: Flowers and scented showers fall from the descending hosts like rain from clouds, and the hill-lord's people come down from the sky, though more slowly than gods descending.
947.nuance: The comparison runs both ways: the host rains flowers like clouds, yet is said to come down a little less than the gods do.
947.event: The Vidyadhara king's host descends from the sky amid falling flowers.

948.reading: The lord of the hill gives an order that the young men, who step on petals, are to walk beside the earth-dwellers on the ground instead of in the air.
948.nuance: The verse is dense and its subject is only 'he of the mountain'; the sense of walking the ground in company is held loosely.
948.event: The Vidyadhara king orders his people to come down and walk on the earth with the others.

949.reading: The host of Vijayan's father spreads like the Ganga to meet the hill-king's host, which comes down like the Yamuna.
949.nuance: The conch-bright one is read as Vijayan, from the epithet used in verse 960; the fathers' hosts are therefore the Podanam king's.
949.event: The Podanam king's host and the Vidyadhara host meet and mingle like two rivers.

950.reading: The mingled sea of troops, with flowers and fly-whisks rising on high, looks like the milk-sea spreading across the sky.

951.reading: Because clouds and young elephants both pour streams, those near must tell them apart for those beside them.
951.nuance: The poet jokes on the confusion of cloud and elephant that the guide's tour in verse 880 had already used.

952.reading: Rows of holy gems, falling flowers and dense banners darken the sides, and the fly-whisk-bearing elephants mingled in them look like a sea coming over the forest ground.

953.reading: Green silk banners spread over the shining gem-set elephants and seem to stand out on them.
953.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 repeat lines 1 and 2 in other verbs; the stanza seems doubled in the source.

954.reading: The scent of aloe wood and musk mixed with the fly-whisks makes the sea-like host seem to come from a fragrant sea.
954.nuance: The aroma is the whole conceit; 'imagiri' in line 4 is read as the fragrant hill-sea and held loosely.

955.reading: The host's colour is like that of women with lovely earrings and bright lips, whose beauty shines in their lion-like men.
955.nuance: The verse repeats lines 1 and 2 as lines 3 and 4; the comparison is unclear and the sense is held loosely.

956.reading: The royal elephants, with gem-set sides and diamond tusks, stand like hills streaming with water.
956.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 repeat lines 1 and 2 with a different ending.

957.reading: The women of the hill-clans have feet so tender that, for a cotton-like cushion laid under them, they start back, and climb up gently with fear.
957.nuance: The subject of the climbing and its object are not clear; the verse seems to speak of the women stepping to mount the elephants.

958.reading: The hill-king and the sceptred lord of the earth meet each other at the hour set by the astrologers, their sea-like hosts standing in order.
958.nuance: The two kings are named by epithets only; the one 'with the order' is read as the earth's king of Podanam.
958.event: The Vidyadhara king and the Podanam king meet at the hour fixed by the astrologers.

959.reading: While the garlanded king's lotus-like hands are closing in salute, the hill-king takes him tightly in his red-flower hands.
959.nuance: The garlanded one is read as the Podanam king; the verse names neither king.
959.event: The Vidyadhara king embraces the other king as he folds his hands.

960.reading: Vijayan and the sea-dark Tivittan fold their hands over their jewelled forearms before the strong-armed king and his bright feet.
960.nuance: The two are named by epithets (the conch-coloured one and the sea-dark youth) and the king they bow to is not named.
960.event: Vijayan and Tivittan bow to the king with folded hands.

961.reading: The king with the lotus-red eyes takes the youths in his gaze, then embraces the younger ones on their golden-hill chests.
961.nuance: Who is 'the elephant-like king' and who are the 'younger ones' is not fixed by the verse.
961.event: The king embraces the young men after greeting them with a look.

962.reading: Arkakirti, son of the lord of the long hills, folds his hands before the golden-anklet feet of the king of Podanam.
962.event: Arkakirti bows to the Podanam king with folded hands.

963.reading: Drinking in his beauty, the king of kings embraces Arkakirti, raises him with himself onto the neck of a young elephant and so seats him.
963.nuance: The seating on the king's own elephant is the sign of honour; nothing in the verse says why Arkakirti is chosen.
963.event: The Podanam king embraces Arkakirti and lifts him onto the neck of his own young elephant.

964.reading: The Vidyadhara king's younger brother and his nephew bow at the anklets of the lord of Suramai, and a swelling flood of love shines through the golden anklets.
964.nuance: The lord of Suramai is read as the Podanam king by another title; 'marukan' may mean nephew or son-in-law and is held loosely.
964.event: The Vidyadhara king's brother and nephew bow at the feet of the lord of Suramai.

965.reading: The hero called Sripalan, the younger father of the one who wields the fierce discus, bows at the feet of the Vidyadhara lord and bows that stainless-famed king's heart as well.
965.nuance: Who Sripalan is, and whose 'younger father' he is, is not clear; the reading is held loosely.
965.event: Sripalan bows at the feet of the Vidyadhara king.

966.reading: After the kings meet, the sea of love overflows like the milk-sea, and with the princes and their love for each other they enter the fair city.
966.nuance: The line 'nectar flood leaped from the sea' makes the meeting itself the source of the love that carries them into the city.
966.event: The kings and princes enter the city after their meeting.

967.reading: The kings and the strong-armed young princes enter the golden palace amid the groves, and women with flower garlands bless them with long-years songs as they reach the Chitrakuta hall.
967.event: The kings and princes enter the palace and reach the Chitrakuta hall.

968.reading: The kings sit like lions on gem-set couches with flower-bearing women fanning chowries and the bright princes beside them.
968.event: The kings sit in the hall with the princes while women fan them.

969.reading: As the women fan chowries that scatter pollen from their hair and bees hum, the lord of the earth speaks, and the verse stops before his words.
969.nuance: The speech is the next verse's, so the speaker is unnamed here and the king of Podanam is only the likely reading.
969.event: The earth's king begins to speak to those seated in the hall.

links.note: Verse 838 has the king raise a host like a sea swallowing the world; verse 949 shows the two hosts meeting as the Ganga and the Yamuna.
links.teaches: The host first likened to a sea is now the river that mingles with another, so the image turns from size to joining.

links.note: Verse 873 has the host's drums and bells roar like the sea as it leaves; verse 950 turns the sea into the milk-sea of the sky.
links.teaches: The sea simile follows the host from departure to meeting, changing from noise to something heavenly and calm.

links.note: Verse 880 has wild elephants mistake clouds for a rival elephant; verse 951 says clouds and young elephants cannot be told apart.
links.teaches: The mistake of cloud for elephant is the beasts' in one verse and the poet's own wit in the other.

links.note: Verse 875 has the host go across the sky past seas and hills; verse 948 gives the order to leave the air and walk the ground.
links.teaches: The sky journey ends in an order of descent, so the aerial tour serves the protocol of a meeting on earth.

links.note: Verse 866 has learned men fix the hour for the bride to board; verse 958 has the kings meet at the hour the astrologers named.
links.teaches: The same trust in the astrologers' hour governs the leaving and the meeting.

links.note: Verse 845 shows Arkakirti standing proudly on his elephant at the head of a host; verse 962 shows him folding his hands to the Podanam king.
links.teaches: The warlord of one scene is shown as a bowing guest in the next, so his pride is placed beneath his courtesy.

links.note: Verse 845 puts Arkakirti on his own elephant; verse 963 has the Podanam king raise him onto the king's own young elephant.
links.teaches: Arkakirti's own elephant is replaced by the host-king's, marking the passage from commander to honoured guest.

links.note: Kural 680 has a small ruler bow to the great out of fear; verse 960 has the princes fold hands before the king at a meeting arranged for a wedding.
links.teaches: The bow of a wedding visit is shown as courtesy between equals, where the couplet sees bowing as a way of buying safety.

gains.a: The verse lacks any reading of the bow as a policy, and the couplet supplies the cold case of a bow from weakness.
gains.b: The couplet lacks a bow made freely by allies who gain nothing by it, which the verse supplies.

links.note: Kural 90 says a guest wilts when the host's face changes on seeing him; verse 963 has the host drink in the guest's beauty and seat him on his own elephant.
links.teaches: The welcome here is warmer than a kept face, since the host shares his own mount, a test the couplet does not set.

gains.a: The verse lacks the couplet's test that a host's welcome is read from the face.
gains.b: The couplet lacks the case of a host who answers by sharing his own seat of rank.

source_issues: 953, 955, 956: lines 3 and 4 repeat lines 1 and 2, so the stanza seems doubled in the source.
947 to 957: the verses are short-metre description with clipped grammar and several readings are held loosely.
958 to 965: the kings and princes are named only by epithets (the hill-king, the conch-coloured, the one with the order) and the identifications are the nearest readings.
965: the printed phrase சிறீ பால னென்பான் has a stray split.
